title: Given the root of a binary tree, return its node values level by level but from the bottom level up to the root, left to right within each level.
shortTitle: Reverse Level Order Traversal (Bottom-up Level Order)
keyPoints: Perform standard BFS (level-order) but add each completed level to the front of the result list.
Using LinkedList.addFirst() is O(1), while ArrayList.add(0, x) is O(n) per insert.
The traversal itself is unchanged; only the accumulation order differs from top-down level order.
An alternative is to collect top-down and reverse the result once at the end.
The technique runs in O(n) time and O(n) space for the queue and result.
The level-size snapshot pattern (poll exactly queue.size() nodes per level) remains the same.

s1_definition.oneliner: Do normal level-order BFS, but add each level to the front of the result so the bottom level comes out first.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Reverse level order** – return node values level by level from the bottom level up to the root.
- **BFS with prepend** – process the tree top-down with a queue, but insert each completed level at the front of the result.
- **LinkedList.addFirst** – O(1) prepend keeps the whole operation linear.
- **Alternative** – collect top-down into an ArrayList and reverse once at the end.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(n) space.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the approval chart must be printed clerks-first, then department heads, then the branch manager at the bottom. You still gather staff rank by rank from the top, but you stack each gathered rank on top of the previous so the last rank gathered prints first.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Tree:     1
         / \
        2   3
       / \
      4   5

BFS processes top-down:
  Level 0: [1]
  Level 1: [2, 3]
  Level 2: [4, 5]

Prepend accumulation:
  After level 0: result = [[1]]
  After level 1: result = [[2,3], [1]]
  After level 2: result = [[4,5], [2,3], [1]]

Final: [[4,5], [2,3], [1]]  (bottom-up)
```

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│     Reverse Level Order Traversal Flow        │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                              │
│   queue = [root]                             │
│       │                                      │
│       ▼                                      │
│   ┌────────────────────────────────┐         │
│   │ While queue is not empty:      │         │
│   │   levelSize = queue.size()     │         │
│   │   for i = 0 to levelSize-1:    │         │
│   │     poll node, record value    │         │
│   │     enqueue children           │         │
│   │   result.addFirst(level)       │ prepend │
│   └────────────────────────────────┘         │
│       │                                      │
│       ▼                                      │
│   return result (bottom-up order)            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Reverse level-order traversal is standard BFS with a single change in how results are accumulated. You process the tree top-down with a queue and the level-size snapshot pattern, but instead of appending each level, you prepend it. Because the bottom level is completed last, prepending puts it first.

The data structure matters: use a LinkedList so that `addFirst()` is O(1). Using an ArrayList and inserting at index zero shifts all existing levels on every insert, silently turning a linear algorithm into a quadratic one.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh produced an audit escalation chart that had to read from the lowest approvers up to the branch head. The tree was naturally traversed top-down, so he ran the standard BFS and prepended each completed level, giving the bottom-up ordering without a second pass.

The insight is that traversal order and accumulation order are independent. BFS always processes top-down; how you store results controls the output.

Remember one sentence: run standard level-order BFS but prepend each level to get bottom-up output.
